content.title: About
content.content: Broccoli casserole with rice is a baked dish that combines tender broccoli florets, cooked rice, a creamy sauce, and cheese. The meal is rich in B‑vitamins, vitamin C, fiber, and plant‑based protein, making it both nutritious and filling.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Broccoli is often called a "mini tree" because its florets resemble tiny crowns.
Casseroles with broccoli have a long tradition in European home cooking, served as a side or a main dish.
The combination of rice and broccoli provides a complete amino‑acid profile, offering a full‑protein option for vegetarians.
Some recipes substitute wild rice for a nuttier flavor and chewier texture.
Broccoli is high in glucosinolates, compounds that support the body’s detoxification processes.

items.title: High in vitamin C
items.content: Broccoli supplies a large amount of vitamin C, which supports immune function and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from both broccoli and rice promotes healthy bowel movements and feeds beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Glucosinolates and carotenoids in broccoli help neutralize free radicals, reducing the risk of chronic disease.

items.title: May lower cholesterol
items.content: Soluble fiber in rice binds bile acids, aiding their excretion and helping lower LDL cholesterol levels.

items.title: Bone health
items.content: Calcium and vitamin K found in broccoli contribute to strong bone structure.

items.title: Broccoli allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to cruciferous vegetables, including broccoli.

items.title: Excessive fiber intake
items.content: Large portions can cause gas and abdominal discomfort in people with sensitive digestion.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Broccoli contains oxalates, which in high amounts may contribute to kidney stone formation.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Cook rice until tender, steam broccoli until just soft, combine with a creamy sauce (milk, cream, flour), stir in shredded cheese, and bake at 180 °C for 20‑25 minutes until the top is golden.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cooled casserole in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat in the oven or microwave until the internal temperature reaches 75 °C.

egg-sandwich-on-biscuit-with-sausage.title: Egg Sandwich on Biscuit with Sausage

content.title: About
content.content: The egg sandwich on biscuit with sausage is a quick breakfast or snack consisting of a soft biscuit, a fried egg, and flavorful sausage. The biscuit provides a light, fluffy base, while the egg and sausage deliver protein and a rich taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Using a biscuit instead of regular bread makes the sandwich lighter and more airy.
The sausage is often made from pork or turkey and seasoned with spices such as paprika and black pepper.
Eggs are typically cooked sunny‑side‑up or scrambled to keep a tender texture.
This sandwich is popular in American diners and fast‑food chains as a classic "breakfast sandwich".
Biscuit‑based sandwiches are easy to pack in paper wrappers for delivery.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Eggs and sausage provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle repair and satiety.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs contain vitamin B12, while sausage adds niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Sausage, especially from red meat, supplies heme iron, which aids oxygen transport.

items.title: Moderate fats
items.content: Fats from the egg and sausage give energy and help absorb fat‑soluble vitamins.

items.title: Calcium from biscuit
items.content: A biscuit made with milk adds a modest amount of calcium beneficial for bones.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Processed sausage often contains a lot of salt, which can be an issue for people with hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Some sausages are rich in saturated fat and should be consumed in moderation.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Egg white is a common allergen; individuals with egg allergy should avoid this product.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The combination of biscuit, egg, and sausage can be calorie‑dense, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Preservatives in sausage
items.content: Certain sausages contain nitrites and other preservatives that may concern sensitive consumers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich is best eaten by hand, split in half. Serve it hot, straight from the pan, or reheat in a microwave. Add fresh lettuce, tomato, or your favorite sauce for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared sandwich in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat in an oven or toaster to restore the biscuit’s crispness before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Pizza without cheese and with a thick crust is a variation of the classic pizza where the traditional cheese is replaced by sauce, vegetables, and spices. The dough is made from flour, water, yeast, and salt, and after baking forms a crunchy yet soft crust. This product is suitable for vegetarians, people with lactose intolerance, and those who prefer lighter flavor combinations.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Thin and thick pizza crusts have different glycemic indexes: a denser crust raises blood sugar more slowly.
The traditional Italian "Marinara" pizza is a cheese‑free version topped with tomato sauce, garlic, and oregano.
Dough for a thick crust is often cold‑fermented for 24–72 hours, enhancing flavor and texture.
In some regions of Russia, a "cheese‑free pizza" is popular and may be served with plant‑based cheese or soy sauce.
A thick crust holds toppings better, allowing generous amounts of vegetables, meat, or seafood without leaking.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain dough provides dietary fiber that supports digestive health.

items.title: Low in lactose
items.content: The absence of cheese makes this pizza suitable for people with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The dough supplies B1, B3, and B6 vitamins important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Antioxidants from tomato sauce
items.content: Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant with anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Versatile toppings
items.content: Adding vegetables, mushrooms, or seafood increases the content of vitamins and minerals.

items.title: High carbohydrate content
items.content: Dough, especially from refined flour, can quickly raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Tomato sauce often contains salt; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional dough contains gluten, which may trigger reactions in individuals with celiac disease.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: A thick crust is more calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable for weight‑managed diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the pizza into serving pieces and serve hot. Add fresh herbs, a drizzle of olive oil, or a spicy sauce to taste. It pairs well with a light arugula and tomato salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days. Reheat in an oven or grill to restore crust crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Rice, white, with corn is a blend of cooked white rice and dried corn, commonly used in baby foods and as a light side dish. The product has a mild flavor, soft texture, and neutral aroma, making it suitable for a variety of meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The rice‑corn blend is frequently used in infant nutrition because both components are easily digestible.
Corn adds a subtle sweetness and an extra source of carbohydrates.
White rice provides fast‑acting carbs that quickly convert to energy.
The mixture is usually steamed, preserving most nutrients.
It is a staple side dish in many Asian and Latin American cuisines.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: The blend delivers a quick source of energy thanks to its high carbohydrate content.

items.title: Easily digestible carbs
items.content: White rice is gentle on the stomach and suitable for people with sensitive digestion.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Rice provides thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, which support metabolism.

items.title: Corn adds dietary fiber
items.content: Corn contributes a modest amount of fiber, aiding digestive health.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The blend contains virtually no fat, making it appropriate for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White rice has a high glycemic index, which can cause rapid blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: Low protein content
items.content: The blend is low in protein and should be paired with other protein sources.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the blend as a side dish with meat, fish, or vegetables, add it to soups, casseroles, or use it as a base for baby purees. Before serving, heat to about 60 °C.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in a sealed package. After opening, use within 3–4 weeks. Discard if any off‑odor, mold, or discoloration appears.

shrimp-and-noodles-with-tomato-sauce.title: Shrimp and noodles with tomato sauce

content.title: About
content.content: The dish “Shrimp and noodles with tomato sauce” combines fresh seafood, delicate noodles, and a fragrant tomato sauce made from ripe tomatoes, onion, garlic, and aromatic herbs. It is a quick, nutritious meal popular in both Asian and Mediterranean cuisines.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomatoes used in the sauce are rich in lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that supports heart health.
Shrimp are one of the most protein‑dense seafood options while being low in fat.
Traditionally the noodles are wheat‑based, but rice or buckwheat noodles can be used for a gluten‑free version.
Fast sautéing of shrimp preserves their tender texture and retains most nutrients.
The dish is often finished with grated Parmesan or fresh herbs, adding extra flavor and aroma.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Shrimp provide a complete set of essential amino acids needed for muscle repair and immune function.

items.title: Low calorie density
items.content: A serving contains roughly 300–350 kcal, making it suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Seafood supplies polyunsaturated fats that support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Lycopene in tomato sauce
items.content: Lycopene has antioxidant properties and may reduce the risk of certain cancers.

items.title: B‑vitamin complex
items.content: Tomatoes and shrimp deliver B12, niacin, and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to shrimp; avoid the dish if allergy is suspected.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Shrimp contain cholesterol, so people with high cholesterol should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Sodium in the sauce
items.content: Tomato sauces are often salted; those with hypertension should monitor sodium intake.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Non‑organic tomatoes may carry pesticide residues; choosing organic produce reduces this risk.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, straight from the pan. Garnish with fresh basil, parsley, or a pinch of chili flakes for extra heat. It pairs well with a slice of whole‑grain bread or a light side salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat gently, adding a splash of water or broth to keep the sauce from drying out. If freezing, omit the noodles, as they can become mushy.

stewed-tripe-with-potatoes-puerto-rican-.title: Stewed Tripe with Potatoes, Puerto Rican Style

content.title: About
content.content: Stewed tripe with potatoes, Puerto Rican style is a traditional Puerto Rican dish featuring beef tripe slowly simmered in a savory tomato‑garlic sauce with olive oil, herbs, and spices, together with chunks of potato. The result is a rich, slightly tangy stew often served with rice or crusty bread.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: In Puerto Rico, tripe ("moco") is considered a delicacy and is frequently prepared for celebrations.
Stewed tripe is high in collagen, which is touted for skin and joint health.
The classic recipe uses an “adobo” blend of garlic, oregano, vinegar, and olive oil.
Potatoes not only make the dish more filling but also mellow the strong flavor of tripe.
The stew is often accompanied by a roasted‑pepper sauce called “moco” that adds extra heat.

items.title: Rich in collagen
items.content: Collagen in tripe supports skin elasticity, hair strength, and joint function.

items.title: Good source of iron
items.content: Beef tripe provides a notable amount of iron, helpful for preventing anemia.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many meat dishes, tripe is relatively low in fat.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The stew supplies vitamin B12 and niacin, essential for nervous system health and metabolism.

items.title: Fiber from potatoes
items.content: Potatoes add dietary fiber, promoting healthy digestion.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beef.

items.title: Digestive heaviness
items.content: Tripe can be tough to digest for people with sensitive stomachs.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: While low in fat, tripe still contains cholesterol, so those with high cholesterol should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Thorough cleaning required
items.content: Improper preparation can leave bacteria; tripe must be well‑washed and boiled before stewing.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the stew hot, typically alongside white rice, beans, or corn bread. Garnish with fresh cilantro or a squeeze of lime for brightness. Leftovers store well in the fridge and can be reheated on the stove or in a microwave.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked stew in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly to a rolling boil before eating to ensure safety.

winter-squash-cooked-no-added-fat.title: Winter squash, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Winter squash (Cucurbita spp.) is a large vegetable rich in beta‑carotene, B‑vitamins, and dietary fiber. When boiled without added fat it retains most nutrients and has a mild, slightly sweet flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Winter squash belongs to the gourd family and is cultivated in many temperate regions worldwide.
Boiled squash is a notable source of beta‑carotene, a provitamin A carotenoid.
Squash has been used in cuisine and traditional medicine since ancient Egypt.
Pumpkin seeds are rich in zinc and magnesium, but they are not part of this product.
Cooking without fat keeps the calorie count low – about 30 kcal per 100 g.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene converts to vitamin A, supporting vision, immune function, and skin health.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Fiber and potassium help regulate blood pressure and cholesterol levels.

items.title: Low calorie density
items.content: Makes it suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Vitamins C and E along with carotenoids protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Digestive health
items.content: Both soluble and insoluble fiber promote regular bowel movements and a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience an allergic reaction to squash.

items.title: Nutrient interactions
items.content: Large portions of squash can slightly inhibit iron absorption from plant sources.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Squash contains modest oxalate levels, which may be relevant for people prone to kidney stones.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Boiled winter squash can be added to soups, purees, salads, porridges, and casseroles. It also works well as a base for sauces or fillings. Serve with fresh herbs, spices, or a squeeze of lemon for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked squash in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3–4 days. For longer keeping, freeze in portion‑size bags – it retains taste and nutrients for up to 3 months.
